vivre-sa-vie-1962.gazette: Twelve numbered tableaux, each headed like an entry in a case file: Godard built the film as a dossier on prostitution in Paris rather than a story about a woman who drifts into it. In one panel the philosopher Brice Parain sits across a café table and talks, unscripted, as himself. The numbering is the claim — that what follows was collected, not composed.

the-big-city-1963.gazette: Calcutta here is a matter of cramped flats, clerks' salaries and the arithmetic of a household that no longer balances. Ray films a wife taking a job selling door to door, and keeps the register close to reportage: the negotiations, the small humiliations, the ledger at the end of the month. A domestic budget is treated as public record.

the-leopard-1963.gazette: Visconti set the film at the exact hinge of 1860 Sicily, when Garibaldi's landing turned into a plebiscite and the old titles began trading against new money. He kept the accounts open: which families rose, which estates were sold, what the unification cost the class it displaced. An aristocrat by birth and a communist by conviction, he shot the transfer of power as bookkeeping rather than pageant.
the-leopard-1963.prism: The catch is that a film about a class losing its grip was made with that class's palaces, silver and tailoring fully intact, so the decline looks magnificent. Accuracy about an ending can end up working as an advertisement for it.

the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew-1965.gazette: Every line spoken in the film comes from Matthew; Pasolini wrote no dialogue of his own. He cast non-professionals and shot in the stone villages of Basilicata and Puglia, standing in for Judea. A Marxist and an atheist made the adaptation the Vatican would later name among its recommended films.

andrei-rublev-1966.gazette: The film moves through episodes taken from the chronicles — the Tatar sack of Vladimir, the long shadow of Kulikovo, the labor of casting a cathedral bell out of clay and molten bronze. Rublev left almost no biography, only icons, so documented history fills in around the silence where a life should be. Finished in 1966, it then sat for years before Soviet audiences were allowed to see it.

au-hasard-balthazar-1966.gazette: Bresson refused the word actor, called the people in his films models, and ran takes until intonation drained out of the lines entirely. The method was a rule about evidence: gesture recorded, expression withheld. At the center of it he placed a donkey, which had no performance to unlearn.
au-hasard-balthazar-1966.prism: Strip out the acting and what remains is behavior, which is exactly why the cruelty in this one registers as fact rather than drama. Nothing is being performed at you; it is simply happening, on camera, at the animal's pace.

bonnie-and-clyde-1967.gazette: The Barrow Gang worked small banks and grocery stores across the Depression Midwest and died in a lawman's ambush on a Louisiana back road in May 1934. Penn's film kept the ambush and rearranged a good deal of the rest, including the Texas Ranger who tracked them; his family later took the studio to court over the portrait. The argument about what the picture owed the record outlasted its box office run.

dont-look-back-1967.gazette: Pennebaker followed Dylan through the 1965 British tour with a hand-held camera and sync sound, then cut what he had: hotel rooms, press conferences, corridors, a piano being tuned. The dates, the halls and the reporters' questions all exist elsewhere in the record, which leaves the film checkable in a way portraits rarely are. It ends when the tour ends.

titicut-follies-1967.gazette: Wiseman took a camera inside Bridgewater State Hospital for the criminally insane in 1966 and came out with force-feedings, strip searches and the inmate variety show that gave the film its name. Massachusetts went to court and won an order restricting it, a rare instance of an American film suppressed by judges on grounds other than obscenity or national security. The conditions on screen outlasted the ban by decades.
titicut-follies-1967.prism: The state argued it was protecting inmate privacy, which meant the men whose treatment was filmed were shielded by making sure nobody saw how they were treated. Suppression on behalf of the filmed is still suppression, and Bridgewater went on operating the entire time.

catch-me-if-you-can-2002.gazette: The film's source is Abagnale's own memoir, a book reporters have spent decades pulling apart; the surviving paper trail supports far less of the pilot-doctor-lawyer résumé than the telling does. Spielberg shot it as a chase anyway, forger and FBI agent circling each other through the early 1960s. The most durable forgery in the case turned out to be the account of it.

capturing-the-friedmans-2003.gazette: The material is almost entirely primary: court records, police accounts, and hours of home video the family shot of itself while the Great Neck case closed in during the late 1980s. Participants sit for interviews and contradict one another on camera, sometimes across a single cut. Every document is verifiable; the story they assemble into is not.

zodiac-2007.gazette: The production went back to police files, newspaper morgues and surviving witnesses rather than to the legend, and left the dead ends standing: jurisdictions that never shared, handwriting that never matched, a suspect who died before anything was proven. Attacks are staged from documented accounts, down to dates, roads and times of day. Nobody has ever been charged with the killings.
zodiac-2007.prism: Build a procedural on a case with no ending and the payoff has to come from the labor itself — the phone calls, the files, the years going by. What gets tracked in the end is the cost to the people doing the tracking, billed by the decade.

of-gods-and-men-2010.gazette: Seven Trappist monks were taken from their monastery at Tibhirine in March 1996 and reported dead two months later, in the worst years of the Algerian civil war. Beauvois assembled the film from what the men left behind — letters, the prior's testament, the fixed daily order of a working monastery — and stops at the abduction rather than following it. Three decades on, responsibility for the killings is still disputed.

snowtown-2011.gazette: Eight bodies in barrels were found in a disused bank vault at Snowtown, South Australia, in May 1999; the killings had run through the northern Adelaide suburbs for most of that decade. Kurzel shot in those suburbs and cast largely out of them, reconstructing the case at the level of kitchens, driveways and back yards instead of investigation rooms. The film withholds almost nothing and explains almost nothing.

the-imposter-2012.gazette: A thirteen-year-old boy vanished from San Antonio in 1994; three years later a Frenchman in his twenties presented himself in Spain as the missing child, and the family flew out and brought him home. Layton runs the documented version — FBI interviews, passport paperwork, a local private investigator's doubts — against the impostor's own narration of how he managed it. The record settles the fraud and settles nothing about the boy.
the-imposter-2012.prism: He got as far as he did because the people around him had their own reasons to accept the story, and reasons like that don't show up in a case file. A con only supplies the lie; the other half has to be something someone already wanted to be true.
